USB Type-C Pinout: Why Are 5.1KΩ Pull-Down Resistors Needed? by: Mila Nov 09,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout USB Type-C pinout 5.1K pull-down resistor USB-C CC pin USB Type-C has become a common interface in modern electronic devices thanks to its reversible design, high-speed data transfer, and high-power delivery capabilities. However, in USB Type-C circuit design , a seemingly simple 5.1KΩ pull-down resistor plays an important role in device identification, connection detection, and power delivery. This article explains how the CC pins work, why two 5.1KΩ resistors are needed, and what to consider when designing a USB Type-C interface. Basic Functions of USB Type-C Pins: Understanding the CC Pins The CC (Configuration Channel) pins are among the most important pins in a USB Type-C connector. They are responsible for several key functions: Device Role Identification: Identify the power source (Source/DFP) and power sink (Sink/UFP). Plug Orientation Detection: Detect the orientation of the USB Type-C plug. Power Capability Identification: Determine the available default power level through the Rp resistor when USB PD is not used. USB PD Communication: Enable bidirectional communication through the CC pins for USB Power Delivery. VCONN Supply: Provide power to electronically marked cables equipped with E-Marker chips. （Type-C CC Pin） The Main Functions of the 5.1KΩ Pull-Down Resistor In a USB Type-C power sink (Sink/UFP), CC1 and CC2 typically each require a separate 5.1KΩ pull-down resistor (Rd) connected to ground. This is the standard resistor-based implementation of Rd and serves several important purposes. 1. Establishing a Defined CC Termination State The pull-down resistor provides a defined termination state for the CC pin. When a Source connects to a Sink, the Source-side pull-up resistor (Rp) and Sink-side pull-down resistor (Rd) form a detection circuit. By monitoring the voltage on the CC pin, the Source can determine whether a compatible Sink device has been connected. 2. Detecting Plug Orientation USB Type-C uses the CC1 and CC2 pins to detect plug orientation. Since the CC wire inside a standard Type-C cable connects to only one of the two CC pins, the Source can monitor their voltage states to identify which pin has an active connection. The interface controller then switches the corresponding data paths to ensure proper operation in either plug orientation. 3. Supporting Power Capability Identification The Source-side Rp and Sink-side Rd establish an electrical connection through the CC pin. By detecting the CC voltage, the Source can identify the connected Sink and determine the appropriate power delivery process. When USB PD is not used, the Source can also indicate its available default current capability through different Rp values. 4. Supporting USB PD Communication When both the Source and Sink support USB Power Delivery (USB PD), they can communicate bidirectionally through the CC pin to negotiate power voltage, current, and other supported functions. How Does the USB Type-C CC Pin Work? Voltage Divider Detection Mechanism The connection detection mechanism of a USB Type-C interface relies on the termination states of its CC pins. The Source-side CC pin is connected to a pull-up supply through Rp, while the Sink-side CC pin is connected to ground through a 5.1KΩ pull-down resistor (Rd). When the two devices are connected, these resistors form a voltage divider. For a resistor-based pull-up implementation, the CC voltage can be calculated using the following formula: Vcc = Vbus × (Rd / (Rp + Rd)) By monitoring the CC voltage, the Source can determine: Whether a compatible Sink device is connected. The type of connected termination. The orientation of the USB Type-C plug. The default power capability available to the Sink. Note that Rp can also be implemented using a current source instead of a resistor. Therefore, the formula above applies primarily to resistor-based pull-up implementations. USB Type-C Device Roles USB Type-C ports can operate in three main roles: Source (DFP): Supplies power and typically uses an Rp pull-up resistor or an equivalent current source for CC detection. Sink (UFP): Receives power and typically uses an Rd pull-down resistor (5.1KΩ) to establish the CC termination. Dual-Role Port (DRP): Can dynamically switch between Source and Sink roles depending on the connection. Plug Orientation Detection A USB Type-C connector has two CC pins, CC1 and CC2. However, in a standard cable connection, only one of them connects to the cable's CC wire. When the plug is inserted in one orientation, the cable's CC wire connects to CC1. When reversed, it connects to CC2. The Source monitors the voltage states of both pins to determine which one has an active connection and identify the plug orientation. The interface controller then switches the corresponding data paths based on the detected orientation, allowing the USB interface to work properly regardless of how the plug is inserted. Power Capability Identification (Without USB PD) Even without USB PD, a USB Type-C interface can indicate its available power capability through the Rp value on the CC pin. In addition to default USB current capabilities, a compliant Source can advertise 5V/1.5A or 5V/3A. These power levels are identified through different Rp resistance values or equivalent current-source implementations. Note: The voltage ranges above represent the corresponding detection ranges for the advertised current levels. Actual designs should follow the applicable USB Type-C specification and controller datasheets. Default USB current capability also depends on the USB connection type and its corresponding specification. Why Must the USB-C 5.1K Resistor Have This Specific Value? USB Type-C Standard Requirements For conventional USB Type-C Sink designs that implement Rd using resistors, 5.1KΩ is the standard pull-down resistance specified by the USB Type-C specification. It allows the Source to correctly identify the Sink connection and initiate the subsequent power delivery process according to the specification. It is important to note that the 5.1KΩ resistor alone does not mean the device supports USB PD communication. USB PD functionality also requires an appropriate protocol controller and physical-layer circuitry. Technical Reasons Specification Compliance: The 5.1KΩ value is the standard Rd resistance. It works with different Source-side Rp values to support the required connection detection mechanism. Reliable Detection: The appropriate pull-down resistance helps keep the CC voltage within the corresponding detection range, allowing the Source to correctly identify the Sink and its available power capability. Compatibility: Using non-standard values such as 10KΩ or 20KΩ may cause the CC voltage to fall outside the specified detection range, preventing some chargers or power sources from correctly identifying the Sink. Distinction from Ra: The USB Type-C specification also defines an Ra resistor, typically ranging from 800Ω to 1200Ω, which is used to identify cables requiring VCONN power. The clear difference between Rd and Ra helps the Source distinguish different connection states. Important Considerations in USB Type-C Circuit Design CC1 and CC2 Must Have Separate Resistors CC1 and CC2 must each have an independent 5.1KΩ pull-down resistor connected to GND. They should not share a single resistor. This is an easily overlooked detail in USB Type-C circuit design . If both CC pins share one pull-down resistor, neither pin can be guaranteed to have its own required Rd termination. When connecting a cable equipped with an E-Marker chip, the cable's Ra termination also participates in CC detection. Sharing one pull-down resistor may cause the Source to misinterpret the combination of Sink and Ra terminations, affecting device connection, cable identification, and VCONN supply. Resistor Tolerance and Package Selection For conventional resistor-based Rd implementations, a 5.1KΩ resistor with 1% tolerance is recommended to ensure stable resistance. Common package sizes include 0603 and 0805. The final selection depends on available PCB space, power dissipation, and assembly requirements. ﻿Common USB Type-C Design Mistakes 1. Missing Pull-Down Resistors: Without proper Rd termination, the Source may fail to detect the Sink device and initiate power delivery. 2. Sharing One Pull-Down Resistor: Connecting CC1 and CC2 to a single resistor may cause plug orientation detection problems and compatibility issues with some E-Marker cables. 3. Using the Wrong Resistance: Non-standard values such as 10KΩ or 20KΩ may cause the CC voltage to fall outside the specified detection range, affecting device identification and power delivery. A Classic Design Mistake: Raspberry Pi 4 （Raspberry Pi 4: Incorrect Type-C Output Pull-Down Resistor Design） The initial version of the Raspberry Pi 4 had a well-known USB Type-C design issue: CC1 and CC2 shared a single 5.1KΩ pull-down resistor instead of having separate pull-down resistors. This design did not comply with the USB Type-C specification. When connected to certain USB Type-C cables equipped with E-Marker chips, the Ra termination inside the cable could interact with the device's resistor network in an unexpected way. As a result, the power source could incorrectly identify the Raspberry Pi as an Audio Adapter Accessory and refuse to supply power. This case demonstrates how even a seemingly minor resistor connection error can affect the compatibility of an entire USB Type-C interface. Raspberry Pi addressed this issue in subsequent hardware revisions by separating the pull-down resistors for CC1 and CC2. （Type C sink; note that CC1 and CC2 are connected separately to 5.1k.） USB PD Communication Through the CC Pin Once the Source detects a valid connection through the 5.1KΩ Rd on the Sink side, it enables VBUS and provides the initial 5V supply. If both the Source and Sink support USB Power Delivery (USB PD), they can communicate bidirectionally through the CC pin to negotiate higher supply voltages (such as 9V, 15V, and 20V) and the corresponding current levels. USB PD uses BMC (Biphase Mark Coding) to transmit data through signal transitions on the CC pin. During this process, the 5.1KΩ pull-down resistor primarily establishes the Sink-side connection termination, while actual PD data communication is handled by the USB PD controller and its CC physical-layer circuitry. Therefore, the 5.1KΩ pull-down resistor is an important part of USB Type-C connection detection, but it is not the only requirement for USB PD communication. Conclusion Although the 5.1KΩ pull-down resistor is a simple passive component, it plays an important role in device identification, connection detection, and power compatibility in USB Type-C interfaces. Configuring separate Rd resistors for CC1 and CC2 allows Sink devices to establish connections according to the USB Type-C specification and communicate correctly with the Source. For PCB engineers, USB Type-C PCB design involves more than connecting data and power lines. Understanding how the CC pins work and properly configuring Rp and Rd resistors are equally important to avoiding device detection and power delivery issues. As USB Type-C and USB PD technologies continue to gain wider adoption, the CC pins remain essential for device connection, power negotiation, and cable identification. Getting these details right is fundamental to improving the reliability and compatibility of USB Type-C interfaces. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. USB Type-C Pinout: Why Are 5.1KΩ Pull-Down Resistors Needed? by: Mila Nov 09,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout USB Type-C pinout 5.1K pull-down resistor USB-C CC pin USB Type-C has become a common interface in modern electronic devices thanks to its reversible design, high-speed data transfer, and high-power delivery capabilities. However, in USB Type-C circuit design , a seemingly simple 5.1KΩ pull-down resistor plays an important role in device identification, connection detection, and power delivery. This article explains how the CC pins work, why two 5.1KΩ resistors are needed, and what to consider when designing a USB Type-C interface. Basic Functions of USB Type-C Pins: Understanding the CC Pins The CC (Configuration Channel) pins are among the most important pins in a USB Type-C connector. They are responsible for several key functions: Device Role Identification: Identify the power source (Source/DFP) and power sink (Sink/UFP). Plug Orientation Detection: Detect the orientation of the USB Type-C plug. Power Capability Identification: Determine the available default power level through the Rp resistor when USB PD is not used. USB PD Communication: Enable bidirectional communication through the CC pins for USB Power Delivery. VCONN Supply: Provide power to electronically marked cables equipped with E-Marker chips. （Type-C CC Pin） The Main Functions of the 5.1KΩ Pull-Down Resistor In a USB Type-C power sink (Sink/UFP), CC1 and CC2 typically each require a separate 5.1KΩ pull-down resistor (Rd) connected to ground. This is the standard resistor-based implementation of Rd and serves several important purposes. 1. Establishing a Defined CC Termination State The pull-down resistor provides a defined termination state for the CC pin. When a Source connects to a Sink, the Source-side pull-up resistor (Rp) and Sink-side pull-down resistor (Rd) form a detection circuit. By monitoring the voltage on the CC pin, the Source can determine whether a compatible Sink device has been connected. 2. Detecting Plug Orientation USB Type-C uses the CC1 and CC2 pins to detect plug orientation. Since the CC wire inside a standard Type-C cable connects to only one of the two CC pins, the Source can monitor their voltage states to identify which pin has an active connection. The interface controller then switches the corresponding data paths to ensure proper operation in either plug orientation. 3. Supporting Power Capability Identification The Source-side Rp and Sink-side Rd establish an electrical connection through the CC pin. By detecting the CC voltage, the Source can identify the connected Sink and determine the appropriate power delivery process. When USB PD is not used, the Source can also indicate its available default current capability through different Rp values. 4. Supporting USB PD Communication When both the Source and Sink support USB Power Delivery (USB PD), they can communicate bidirectionally through the CC pin to negotiate power voltage, current, and other supported functions. How Does the USB Type-C CC Pin Work? Voltage Divider Detection Mechanism The connection detection mechanism of a USB Type-C interface relies on the termination states of its CC pins. The Source-side CC pin is connected to a pull-up supply through Rp, while the Sink-side CC pin is connected to ground through a 5.1KΩ pull-down resistor (Rd). When the two devices are connected, these resistors form a voltage divider. For a resistor-based pull-up implementation, the CC voltage can be calculated using the following formula: Vcc = Vbus × (Rd / (Rp + Rd)) By monitoring the CC voltage, the Source can determine: Whether a compatible Sink device is connected. The type of connected termination. The orientation of the USB Type-C plug. The default power capability available to the Sink. Note that Rp can also be implemented using a current source instead of a resistor. Therefore, the formula above applies primarily to resistor-based pull-up implementations. USB Type-C Device Roles USB Type-C ports can operate in three main roles: Source (DFP): Supplies power and typically uses an Rp pull-up resistor or an equivalent current source for CC detection. Sink (UFP): Receives power and typically uses an Rd pull-down resistor (5.1KΩ) to establish the CC termination. Dual-Role Port (DRP): Can dynamically switch between Source and Sink roles depending on the connection. Plug Orientation Detection A USB Type-C connector has two CC pins, CC1 and CC2. However, in a standard cable connection, only one of them connects to the cable's CC wire. When the plug is inserted in one orientation, the cable's CC wire connects to CC1. When reversed, it connects to CC2. The Source monitors the voltage states of both pins to determine which one has an active connection and identify the plug orientation. The interface controller then switches the corresponding data paths based on the detected orientation, allowing the USB interface to work properly regardless of how the plug is inserted. Power Capability Identification (Without USB PD) Even without USB PD, a USB Type-C interface can indicate its available power capability through the Rp value on the CC pin. In addition to default USB current capabilities, a compliant Source can advertise 5V/1.5A or 5V/3A. These power levels are identified through different Rp resistance values or equivalent current-source implementations. Note: The voltage ranges above represent the corresponding detection ranges for the advertised current levels. Actual designs should follow the applicable USB Type-C specification and controller datasheets. Default USB current capability also depends on the USB connection type and its corresponding specification. Why Must the USB-C 5.1K Resistor Have This Specific Value? USB Type-C Standard Requirements For conventional USB Type-C Sink designs that implement Rd using resistors, 5.1KΩ is the standard pull-down resistance specified by the USB Type-C specification. It allows the Source to correctly identify the Sink connection and initiate the subsequent power delivery process according to the specification. It is important to note that the 5.1KΩ resistor alone does not mean the device supports USB PD communication. USB PD functionality also requires an appropriate protocol controller and physical-layer circuitry. Technical Reasons Specification Compliance: The 5.1KΩ value is the standard Rd resistance. It works with different Source-side Rp values to support the required connection detection mechanism. Reliable Detection: The appropriate pull-down resistance helps keep the CC voltage within the corresponding detection range, allowing the Source to correctly identify the Sink and its available power capability. Compatibility: Using non-standard values such as 10KΩ or 20KΩ may cause the CC voltage to fall outside the specified detection range, preventing some chargers or power sources from correctly identifying the Sink. Distinction from Ra: The USB Type-C specification also defines an Ra resistor, typically ranging from 800Ω to 1200Ω, which is used to identify cables requiring VCONN power. The clear difference between Rd and Ra helps the Source distinguish different connection states. Important Considerations in USB Type-C Circuit Design CC1 and CC2 Must Have Separate Resistors CC1 and CC2 must each have an independent 5.1KΩ pull-down resistor connected to GND. They should not share a single resistor. This is an easily overlooked detail in USB Type-C circuit design . If both CC pins share one pull-down resistor, neither pin can be guaranteed to have its own required Rd termination. When connecting a cable equipped with an E-Marker chip, the cable's Ra termination also participates in CC detection. Sharing one pull-down resistor may cause the Source to misinterpret the combination of Sink and Ra terminations, affecting device connection, cable identification, and VCONN supply. Resistor Tolerance and Package Selection For conventional resistor-based Rd implementations, a 5.1KΩ resistor with 1% tolerance is recommended to ensure stable resistance. Common package sizes include 0603 and 0805. The final selection depends on available PCB space, power dissipation, and assembly requirements. ﻿Common USB Type-C Design Mistakes 1. Missing Pull-Down Resistors: Without proper Rd termination, the Source may fail to detect the Sink device and initiate power delivery. 2. Sharing One Pull-Down Resistor: Connecting CC1 and CC2 to a single resistor may cause plug orientation detection problems and compatibility issues with some E-Marker cables. 3. Using the Wrong Resistance: Non-standard values such as 10KΩ or 20KΩ may cause the CC voltage to fall outside the specified detection range, affecting device identification and power delivery. A Classic Design Mistake: Raspberry Pi 4 （Raspberry Pi 4: Incorrect Type-C Output Pull-Down Resistor Design） The initial version of the Raspberry Pi 4 had a well-known USB Type-C design issue: CC1 and CC2 shared a single 5.1KΩ pull-down resistor instead of having separate pull-down resistors. This design did not comply with the USB Type-C specification. When connected to certain USB Type-C cables equipped with E-Marker chips, the Ra termination inside the cable could interact with the device's resistor network in an unexpected way. As a result, the power source could incorrectly identify the Raspberry Pi as an Audio Adapter Accessory and refuse to supply power. This case demonstrates how even a seemingly minor resistor connection error can affect the compatibility of an entire USB Type-C interface. Raspberry Pi addressed this issue in subsequent hardware revisions by separating the pull-down resistors for CC1 and CC2. （Type C sink; note that CC1 and CC2 are connected separately to 5.1k.） USB PD Communication Through the CC Pin Once the Source detects a valid connection through the 5.1KΩ Rd on the Sink side, it enables VBUS and provides the initial 5V supply. If both the Source and Sink support USB Power Delivery (USB PD), they can communicate bidirectionally through the CC pin to negotiate higher supply voltages (such as 9V, 15V, and 20V) and the corresponding current levels. USB PD uses BMC (Biphase Mark Coding) to transmit data through signal transitions on the CC pin. During this process, the 5.1KΩ pull-down resistor primarily establishes the Sink-side connection termination, while actual PD data communication is handled by the USB PD controller and its CC physical-layer circuitry. Therefore, the 5.1KΩ pull-down resistor is an important part of USB Type-C connection detection, but it is not the only requirement for USB PD communication. Conclusion Although the 5.1KΩ pull-down resistor is a simple passive component, it plays an important role in device identification, connection detection, and power compatibility in USB Type-C interfaces. Configuring separate Rd resistors for CC1 and CC2 allows Sink devices to establish connections according to the USB Type-C specification and communicate correctly with the Source. For PCB engineers, USB Type-C PCB design involves more than connecting data and power lines. Understanding how the CC pins work and properly configuring Rp and Rd resistors are equally important to avoiding device detection and power delivery issues. As USB Type-C and USB PD technologies continue to gain wider adoption, the CC pins remain essential for device connection, power negotiation, and cable identification. Getting these details right is fundamental to improving the reliability and compatibility of USB Type-C interfaces. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Why Are Two MOSFETs Connected Back-to-Back in a MOSFET Circuit? by: Mila Nov 12,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout mosfet circuit MOSFET Body Diode Back-to-Back MOSFETs Bidirectional MOSFET Switch Reverse Current Blocking In PCB design , MOSFETs are widely used in power management circuits to control current flow, protect power sources, and manage power switching. However, when a circuit needs to support both charging and discharging while preventing unwanted reverse current, a single MOSFET may not be sufficient. This is where two back-to-back MOSFETs come into play. By connecting two MOSFETs in series with oppositely oriented body diodes, designers can create a bidirectional switch that allows current to flow in both directions when turned on and blocks current in either direction when turned off. This article explains how this configuration works and why it is useful in PCB power circuit design. 1. What Is a Bidirectional Switch? A bidirectional switch is a switching circuit built using MOSFETs, IGBTs, or other power semiconductor devices. It allows current to flow in either direction when turned on and blocks current in both directions when turned off. For example, when point A has a positive voltage and point B has a negative voltage, current can flow from A to B. When the voltage polarity reverses, with A becoming negative and B positive, the current direction also reverses, allowing current to flow from B to A. A bidirectional switch can be constructed by connecting two MOSFETs or IGBTs back-to-back. （Back-to-back MOSFET circuit） So, how does this configuration allow current to flow in both directions? 2. How Do Back-to-Back MOSFETs Enable Bidirectional Conduction? Let's use a circuit that supports both USB-to-battery charging and battery-to-USB power delivery as an example. Charging the Battery from USB When the USB power source charges the battery, the USB-side voltage is higher than the battery-side voltage. In this condition, Q3 turns on, and the USB power source establishes an initial current path through the body diode of Q1 and Q3. The control circuit then applies sufficient gate drive voltage to Q1 and Q2, turning both MOSFETs on. Once both MOSFETs are on, current flows through their conducting channels to the battery, allowing it to charge. Powering a USB Load from the Battery When the battery supplies power to an external USB load, the current flows in the opposite direction. Q3 turns on, allowing an initial current path to form through the body diode of Q2 and Q3. The control circuit then drives Q1 and Q2 on, allowing current to flow through both MOSFET channels toward the USB interface and power the external load. Blocking Reverse Current When Turned Off When Q3 is turned off, the charging and discharging paths are interrupted. The USB power source can no longer charge the battery, and the battery can no longer supply power to the external USB load. This provides reverse current blocking, also known as reverse current protection, preventing unwanted current from flowing back into the power source. It is important to note that the body diode does not automatically turn on the MOSFET channel. Actual MOSFET conduction depends on the gate-to-source voltage (VGS) and the control circuit's operating logic. （The Principle of Reverse Current Blocking） 3. Why Use Two Back-to-Back MOSFETs Instead of One? To understand this, we first need to look at an important MOSFET characteristic: the body diode. A MOSFET has an intrinsic body diode. In a typical N-channel enhancement-mode MOSFET, the body diode's anode is connected to the source (S), and its cathode is connected to the drain (D). This means that even when the MOSFET is turned off, its body diode can still conduct current under the right voltage conditions. Using a Single MOSFET When only one MOSFET is used, turning it off closes its conducting channel, but the body diode remains present. For example, suppose the battery is connected to the source side of the MOSFET and the external load is connected to the drain side. If the source voltage becomes higher than the drain voltage by enough to forward-bias the body diode, the diode conducts. Current can still flow from the battery to the external load through the body diode, so the MOSFET cannot fully block current in this direction. Therefore, a single MOSFET can conduct current in both directions when turned on, but it cannot block current in both directions when turned off. Using Two Back-to-Back MOSFETs When two MOSFETs are connected back-to-back, their body diodes face opposite directions. When both MOSFETs are turned on, their conducting channels are enabled, allowing current to flow from either side to the other. This provides bidirectional conduction. When both MOSFETs are turned off, the oppositely oriented body diodes provide bidirectional blocking. Regardless of which side has the higher voltage, one of the body diodes will be reverse-biased, preventing current from flowing through the series path. Therefore, two back-to-back MOSFETs can provide both bidirectional conduction and bidirectional blocking. Single MOSFET vs. Back-to-Back MOSFETs The main differences between these two configurations can be summarized as follows: （Single MOSFET vs. Back-to-Back MOSFETs） Conclusion Back-to-back MOSFETs provide an effective way to achieve bidirectional switching and reverse current blocking in power management circuits. Unlike a single MOSFET, this configuration can block current in either direction when turned off while allowing bidirectional conduction when both MOSFETs are on. For PCB design , understanding MOSFET body diode orientation and the operating states of each MOSFET is essential when designing battery charging and discharging circuits, power-path management systems, and other applications that require reliable current control. Proper component selection and gate-drive control are also important to ensure the circuit operates as intended. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Verify Now Blog > Why Should a Decoupling Capacitor Be Placed Close to the IC Why Should a Decoupling Capacitor Be Placed Close to the IC by: Mila Nov 10,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout Decoupling Capacitor Decoupling Capacitor Placement Decoupling Capacitor Layout PCB Decoupling Capacitor “Decoupling capacitors should be placed as close to the IC as possible.” Almost every electronics design textbook emphasizes this rule. However, few explain exactly why the distance matters. If this is treated as a rule to memorize rather than a design principle to understand, it can be difficult to apply it effectively when layout problems arise. To understand why placement matters, we need to look at three key factors: parasitic inductance, capacitor equivalent series inductance (ESL), and current loop design. This article explores how decoupling capacitor placement affects circuit performance through simulation and practical PCB layout examples. 1. What Is a Decoupling Capacitor? The IC's Instantaneous Power Source Simply put, a decoupling capacitor (also known as a bypass capacitor) acts as a local energy storage unit. When an IC experiences a transient current demand, the capacitor can quickly supply the required current, helping maintain a stable supply voltage. When digital ICs switch logic states, their internal transistors switch rapidly and draw brief bursts of current from the power supply. If this current must be delivered entirely by a remote power source through long PCB traces, the parasitic inductance in the power and ground paths will oppose rapid changes in current. This can cause supply voltage drops, ground potential fluctuations, and other issues, including ground bounce. When a decoupling capacitor is placed close to the IC's power pin, the IC can draw charge from the nearby capacitor to meet transient current demands instead of relying entirely on the remote power supply. Because the current loop between the capacitor and the IC is shorter, its parasitic inductance is lower, helping reduce power supply voltage fluctuations. （A decoupling capacitor placed close to the IC supplies transient current during switching operations.） PCB traces between the capacitor and the IC inevitably introduce parasitic inductance. In general, the farther apart they are, the greater the parasitic inductance contributed by the traces. This trace-induced inductance is referred to as Lwire throughout this article. The trace inductance and the capacitor's own equivalent series inductance (ESL) jointly affect the entire decoupling loop. At high frequencies, inductive reactance increases with frequency, making it more difficult for the capacitor to deliver current quickly. In other words, the farther the capacitor is from the IC, the greater the parasitic inductance in the current loop is likely to be, and the less effective the capacitor becomes at high-frequency decoupling. 2. Capacitors Also Have Parasitic Inductance There is another important factor to consider: the capacitor itself has an equivalent series inductance (ESL), denoted as Lesl. A capacitor's ESL depends on its package size, internal construction, and mounting method. Generally, surface-mount ceramic capacitors have relatively low ESL because they do not have long leads. Through-hole capacitors, on the other hand, typically have higher ESL due to the additional inductance introduced by their leads and mounting paths. Because of ESL, every capacitor has an effective self-resonant frequency (SRF). The self-resonant frequency can be approximately calculated using the following formula: Where: L is the capacitor's equivalent series inductance (ESL). C is the capacitance. Below the self-resonant frequency, the capacitor behaves primarily as a capacitive element. At the self-resonant frequency, its impedance reaches a minimum. Above this frequency, the capacitor behaves primarily as an inductor. This is one reason why surface-mount ceramic capacitors are preferred for decoupling applications. Their relatively low ESL allows them to maintain capacitive behavior over a wider frequency range. The two parasitic inductances mentioned above—trace inductance Lwire and the capacitor's own ESL (Lesl)—can be modeled as series inductances in a simplified equivalent circuit. Together with the capacitance C, they form an LC network that affects the overall performance of the decoupling loop. In an actual PCB design, other parasitic elements introduced by the power and ground paths, pads, and vias must also be taken into account. (Equivalent circuit of a decoupling capacitor.) Trace parasitic inductance Lwire and the capacitor's equivalent series inductance Lesl jointly affect the high-frequency performance of the decoupling loop. 3. Simulation: How Does Placement Distance Affect Decoupling Performance? Varying the Distance Between the Decoupling Capacitor and the IC Simulation provides a straightforward way to observe how changes in capacitor placement distance affect power supply voltage fluctuations. The simulation parameters are as follows: Voltage source: Supply voltage VCC = 3.3 V. Current source: Simulates IC switching activity with a 1 ns rise time. Inductor: Represents the trace inductance Lwire between the IC and the capacitor. Decoupling capacitor: C = 0.1 μF, with an equivalent series inductance (ESL) of 1 nH. Measurement point: Voltage at the IC's power supply pin. (Simulation circuit schematic) Different placement distances between the IC and the capacitor are simulated by varying Lwire. （Simulation results with different trace inductance values） The simulation waveforms lead to the following conclusions: The closer the capacitor is to the IC, the smaller Lwire becomes. This generally reduces parasitic inductance in the current loop and improves power supply voltage stabilization. When the capacitor is placed too far away, additional trace inductance increases high-frequency impedance, reducing the capacitor's ability to respond to the IC's transient current demands. As trace inductance increases, the resonant frequency of the LC loop decreases, resulting in a longer ringing period. Varying the Capacitance Increasing capacitance helps suppress lower-frequency voltage fluctuations, but high-frequency performance does not necessarily improve due to ESL limitations. The simulation results show that increasing capacitance allows the capacitor to store more charge. Under otherwise identical conditions, this can help reduce voltage fluctuations at lower frequencies. However, this does not mean that a larger capacitor always provides better high-frequency decoupling. The capacitor's ESL limits its high-frequency performance. Once the operating frequency exceeds the self-resonant frequency, the capacitor behaves primarily as an inductor. Increasing capacitance alone may therefore not improve high-frequency decoupling. When selecting decoupling capacitors, capacitance should not be the only consideration. ESL and the target operating frequency must also be taken into account. 4. Multi-Level Decoupling for Better Power Integrity A single decoupling capacitor cannot effectively cover a wide frequency range. In practice, capacitors with different capacitance values are usually placed at different locations in the power distribution network to meet decoupling requirements across multiple frequency ranges. Level 1: At the PCB Power Input or Voltage Regulator Output (Energy Storage and Low-Frequency Support) These capacitors are typically placed near the power input or voltage regulator output. Their main functions include: Providing additional charge storage to support load variations. Reducing power supply voltage fluctuations at lower frequencies. Working with filtering circuits, when necessary, to suppress external power supply noise. Component selection: Aluminum electrolytic or tantalum capacitors with capacitance values in the tens of microfarads are commonly used. An LC filter can also be added when necessary. Level 2: Close to the IC Power Pins (High-Frequency Decoupling) These capacitors are placed close to the IC's power and ground pins. Their main functions include: Supplying local transient current during IC switching operations. Reducing the impedance of high-frequency current loops. Minimizing transient voltage fluctuations in the power and ground paths. Component selection: Surface-mount ceramic capacitors, typically ranging from 0.01 μF to 0.1 μF, are commonly used. Low-ESL models are preferred. The actual capacitance and number of capacitors should be determined based on the IC datasheet and power integrity requirements. As a general starting point, one decoupling capacitor per IC can be considered. For low-speed, low-current ICs, multiple devices may also share a single capacitor if the power distribution network and current loop are properly designed. The first level provides energy storage and low-frequency power support, while the second level suppresses high-frequency transient noise near the IC. 5. Practical PCB Decoupling Capacitor Layout Guidelines How Close Is Close Enough? As a general guideline, when space allows, the distance between a decoupling capacitor and the IC's power and ground pins should ideally be kept within 2–3 mm. However, this is only a practical reference for some conventional designs, not a universal design standard. For high-speed digital circuits, RF circuits, and other applications with demanding power integrity requirements, the layout recommendations provided by the IC manufacturer should take priority. It is also important to understand that physical proximity alone does not guarantee effective decoupling. What really matters is keeping the actual current path as short as possible. Even if a capacitor is physically placed right next to an IC, routing the power and ground traces along unnecessarily long paths can still create a large current loop. This increases parasitic inductance and reduces decoupling effectiveness. Conversely, even if there is a small physical gap between the components, a direct connection with a sufficiently short current loop can still provide good decoupling performance. When evaluating decoupling layouts, do not focus solely on the physical distance between components. Pay attention to the length of the complete current loop and its associated parasitic inductance. (Poor layout example) Although the components appear close together, winding traces unnecessarily extend the actual current path. The effectiveness of a decoupling capacitor should be evaluated based on the actual current loop. Pay Attention to the Ground Via In multilayer PCB designs, the via connecting the capacitor's ground terminal to the ground plane should be placed as close as possible to the capacitor's ground pad. When the design allows, the via can be placed directly next to the pad or implemented using an appropriate via-in-pad design. If the via is too far from the pad, the connecting trace also introduces parasitic inductance, increasing the impedance of the current loop. When space permits, one or more ground vias can be placed near the capacitor's ground pad to shorten the connection to the ground plane. At the same time, avoid unnecessary vias or routing between the IC's power pin and the decoupling capacitor to keep the entire current loop as short as possible. Conclusion Effective decoupling requires more than simply placing a capacitor near an IC. Capacitance, ESL, placement, and current loop design all affect power supply stability. By understanding how these factors interact and applying proper PCB layout techniques, you can reduce power supply noise and improve overall circuit performance. Talking about the Composition of PCB Price Over the years, PCB price changes have been familiar with people inside and outside the industry, even though some people with years of experience in the PCB industry may not fully understand the ins and outs of this, so to analyze the main factors affecting pcb price: The diversity of prices caused by the different materials used in PCBs is based on common double-sided boards. Sheets generally include fr-4, cem-3, etc., and board thickness varies from 0.2mm to 5.0mm, and copper thickness varies from 0.5oz to 3oz. All of these have resulted in huge price differences on the sheet material; in solder mask inks, there are also certain price differences between ordinary thermoset oils and photosensitive green oils, and thus the diversity of materials has caused price diversity. The different production processes used by PCBs result in different production processes with different prices that will result in different costs. Such as gold-plated plates and sprayed tin plates, the production of the shape of the milling (milling) plate and beer (red) plate, the use of silk screen lines and dry film lines will have different costs, resulting in a variety of prices. The diversity of prices caused by the difficulty of the PCB itself Even if the material is the same, the process is the same, but the difficulty of the PCB itself will result in different costs. For example, if there are 1000 holes on both boards, the hole diameter of one board is more than 0.6mm and the hole diameter of the other board is less than 0.6mm, different drilling costs will be formed; if the two boards are the same, the linewidth is different. Differently, one type is larger than 0.2mm and one type is smaller than 0.2mm, which also causes different production costs, because the scrap rate of difficult plates is high, the inevitable cost is increased, and the price diversity is thus caused. Different customer requirements will also cause different prices The level of customer demand will directly affect the plate production rate, such as a board by ipc-a-600e, class1 requirements have a 98% pass rate, but according to class3 requirements may be only 90% The passing rate, resulting in different costs for the mill, eventually led to a change in the price of the product. The diversity of prices caused by different PCB manufacturers even if the same product, but because of different manufacturers of technology and equipment, different levels of technology, will also form a different cost, nowadays many manufacturers like to produce tin spray plate, because the process is simple, low cost, but Some manufacturers also produce gold-plated plates, resulting in higher scrap rates and higher costs. Therefore, they prefer to produce tin-spray plates, so their prices for tin-spray plates are lower than those for gold-plated plates. The price difference caused by different payment methods At present, PCB manufacturers generally adjust PCB prices according to different payment methods, ranging from 5% to 10%, which also results in price differences. Diversification of prices caused by regional differences At present, from the geographical point of view, prices have been increasing from south to north. There are certain differences in prices in different regions, and thus different regions have also caused price diversity. events.before: Resources Case Studies Case Study: NASA Partners with Xometry to Fast-track Critical Life Support Systems on the International Space Station Case Study: NASA Partners with Xometry to Fast-track Critical Life Support Systems on the International Space Station Written by Serena Ngoh 4 min read Published October 9, 2020 NASA engineers at the Marshall Space Flight Center employed Xometry’s large format CNC machining capabilities to build mission-critical air purification units. At a Glance Industry Manufacturing Services Utilized Project Brief Solution Industry ☑ Aerospace & Defense ☐ Automotive ☐ Consumer Products ☐ Education ☐ Electronics and Semiconductors ☐ Energy ☐ Industrial ☐ Medical & Dental ☐ Robotics ☐ Supply Chain & Purchasing Manufacturing Services Utilized ☑ CNC Machining ☐ Sheet Metal Fabrication ☐ 3D Printing ☐ Urethane Casting ☐ Injection Molding ☐ Die Casting and Extrusion ☑ Post-Processing ☑ Inspection Services Project Brief NASA needed to fast-track the production of components for an air purification unit for the International Space Station. Expedited manufacturing would help the team remain on its proposed rocket launch schedule. Solution Xometry sourced uncommonly large stock material and CNC machined 2 single body vessels with extremely tight tolerances and critical sealing surfaces—all within a 4-week lead time. Xometry reduced the projected lead time by 2 months and decreased costs by 75%, enabling future flexible and comprehensive design methodologies. What Do You Need to Live In Space? Recyclable Energy Systems. On the International Space Station (ISS), critical resources are maintained in closed-loop systems. These systems replenish resources such as oxygen and water, which allows NASA astronauts to live 220 miles (350 km) above the earth. The design, fabrication, and maintenance of these systems is the job of NASA’s Environmental Control and Life Support Systems (ECLSS) team. The latest project that ECLSS engineers at the Marshall Space Flight Center (MSFC) in Huntsville, Alabama, are working on is an air purification unit that will scrub carbon dioxide from the air via a desiccant (a material that draws water from air) and a molecular sieve (a material that traps and expels carbon dioxide molecules outside the space station). This system is known as the Four Bed Carbon Dioxide Scrubber (4BCO2) system. The Challenge: Building Extra Large Flight Components at Record Speeds Over the last 2 years, the design of the 4BCO2 system has progressed using a multi-part design for the cylindrical bed hardware. This design required the parts to be welded together. As the manufacturing process began on the cylindrical beds—the foundational components of the system—ECLSS engineers ran into a problem. It was determined that the welding operations (the best method for NASA’s in-house capabilities), would introduce delays due to a lengthy weld certification process. This posed significant risk to the team’s ability to meet their hardware delivery schedule. Due the schedule risk, the ECLSS team decided to abandon the welded design and associated weld certification process and explore other design options. Redesigning the parts by reducing the size of the beds was not an option as it would compromise the system’s functional performance. Instead, the team decided on a one-piece barrel design. This decision required the fabrication to be outsourced in order to get the priority needed to maintain schedule. The 4BCO2 team, led by NASA engineer Jimmy Hill, reached out to Xometry to see if the company could handle this highly custom job. CAD assembly of the air purification units “Xometry’s supplier management passes savings on to us. Parts are so fast and cheap that we can change the way we work and design.” Jimmy Hill Lead mechanical design engineer at NASA Marshall Space Flight Center A Highly Custom CNC Machining Solution Hill spoke with Xometry’s dedicated account representatives about the project requirements and timeline, emphasizing that the project was now behind schedule. Hill requested a 4-week turnaround, which would involve sourcing a specialized, large-format CNC machine shop in Xometry’s ITAR-certified network. Within the allotted 4 weeks, Xometry secured rare, specialty heat-treated, cylindrical aluminum stock as well as a Manufacturing Partner to make the 12” by 16” diameter parts. The parts were carefully machined to aerospace standards, including tight tolerances of 0.005” and accuracy to GD&T. Critical sealing surfaces of the pressure vessel were machined with o-ring grooves, close-fitting parts, tight side and positional control tolerances, and highly accurate tapped and thru-holes. The Xometry inspection team verified the parts via CMM inspection before passing the parts on to NASA for the verification testing process. From there, the parts passed all of NASA’s individual material tests as well as the full integration tests. “We asked for a lot, and Xometry did an amazing job. Your CNC machining service saved the day.” Jimmy Hill Lead mechanical design engineer at NASA Marshall Space Flight Center Xometry CNC machined 4 vessel components to make 2 air purification units for the NASA International Space Station Xometry has a video version of this case study. Watch It Now Xometry Manufacturing Is Changing the Way NASA Develops Parts With help from Xometry’s on-demand manufacturing services, the air purification unit developed by NASA’s ECLSS team is on track to go up in the Cygnus rocket during the NG-15 launch in 2021. Xometry’s turnkey services reduced what would have been a 3-month in-house production timeline to just one month, preventing a domino effect of delays. Hill says that Xometry’s market-accurate pricing and supplier management allows NASA to save 3-4 times the projected cost of in-house manufacturing. And because of the high-cost savings, the team’s development methodology can shift from linear prototyping to a more lean, parallel prototyping methodology. This has the effect of dramatically reducing project lead times. “We typically have a lot of internal overhead with paperwork and personnel costs, but Xometry’s time-saving supplier management passes on savings to us. Xometry has capabilities that we don’t have in-house, and is so fast and cheap that we don’t mind paying for 2 or 3 [flight equivalent] versions at once. This helps us gain time in our schedule,” says Hill. With the success of the air purification unit and various other jobs, NASA teams across 10 US facilities are confident that Xometry can take on mission-critical work for all types of machined, sheet metal, or 3D printed parts. “Because of Xometry’s flexibility, speed, and quality, all of our projects now look to Xometry for cost effective supply of space flight hardware for life support systems.” David Jones ECLSS Integration & Development Lead at Marshall Space Flight Center Serena Ngoh I write about Xometry and all things manufacturing. You might also see me hosting webinars, designing infographics, producing videos, and working directly with customers to tell their manufacturing success stories. events.before: Resources Case Studies Coastal Range Pivots Camping Stove Design With Custom Parts From Xometry Coastal Range Pivots Camping Stove Design With Custom Parts From Xometry 3 min read Published November 12, 2026 By leveraging Xometry’s on-demand supplier network, Coastal Range secured precision brass and aluminum prototypes in just two weeks to debut an improved stove design at a key trade show. John Peretti founded Coastal Range Equipment to create the gear he knew hikers and backpackers were looking for. After spending five years running research and development for a leading camping stove company, Peretti knew that people wanted a small, lightweight camping stove that didn’t sacrifice quality or capacity. He designed his company’s first product, the Backpacker Ultralight Stove, and machined the prototype parts himself so he could put the stove through rigorous testing to get ready for its first production run. The Backpacker was successfully funded on Kickstarter in 2025, and Peretti is continuing to tweak the design in preparation for a larger rollout. The Challenge: Adjusting Product Design in Time for a Key Trade Show Testing and early customer feedback on the Backpacker showed that the stove's internal valve assembly needed some adjustments. The original assembly relied on a brass fitting that was pressed in and crimped into place, which could cause fuel leaks if it became loose. Replacing it with a threaded connection would simplify manufacturing and significantly upgrade flame control. Peretti hoped to have the updated design ready to show off at the Grassroots Outdoor Alliance trade show in Kansas City. With the show just weeks away, he was worried that the overseas manufacturer he usually works with wouldn’t be able to hit the deadline. Backed up with other orders and facing upcoming holidays, Peretti’s primary vendor said they couldn’t deliver the new parts in less than six weeks. Waiting for the parts would mean Peretti couldn’t bring physical proof of concept to the trade show. Peretti uploaded his CAD drawing to the Xometry Instant Quoting Engine® to order custom components for the Coastal Range camping stove, including a newly engineered brass spindle, threaded brass lip, and aluminum valve body. (Image credit: John Peretti) The Solution: Xometry Creates Custom Parts on Demand To secure the parts he needed on a faster timeline, Peretti brought his designs to Xometry. He was already familiar with Xometry’s manufacturing capabilities, having previously sourced 3D-printed plastic concept models and metal 3D-printed functional samples for early iterations of the stove. When he needed quick-turn, production-grade parts, he turned back to Xometry for CNC machining. Peretti ordered the custom components, including a newly engineered brass spindle, threaded brass lip, and aluminum valve body. The Xometry Instant Quoting Engine® made it easy to upload his CAD drawings, get a price and lead time, and get the designs reviewed for manufacturability. Getting the parts in sooner … meant that if it hadn't worked, I would have had time to quickly spin a revision. And with that extra time … I was able to do targeted outreach to prospective customers attending this trade show to say, ‘Hey, I’ve got new stuff to show. Come by our booth. John Peretti Founder and CEO The Results: High-Quality Parts, With Time to Spare While Coastal Range’s usual production factory estimated it would take six weeks or more to deliver the revised components, Xometry delivered the finished parts in two weeks. Xometry’s network of more than 5,000 vetted manufacturing suppliers gives customers access to manufacturing capacity across the globe, so if one supplier or region is experiencing delays, it doesn’t result in longer wait times or missed deadlines. “I think I got these parts two weeks early,” Peretti said. “So the turnaround time was really fantastic … better than promised by quite a bit. It meets or exceeds on all the dimensions that matter to me — price and turnaround, and the quality is very good.” Receiving the parts well ahead of schedule gave Peretti the buffer he needed to be ready for the trade show. He had time to validate the new valve design, assemble fully functional trade show samples, and start booking targeted retailer meetings before the event. “Getting the parts in sooner … meant that if it hadn't worked, I would have had time to quickly spin a revision,” Peretti said. “And with that extra time … I was able to do targeted outreach to prospective customers attending this trade show to say, ‘Hey, I’ve got new stuff to show. Come by our booth’”. By tapping into Xometry’s on-demand manufacturing capacity, Coastal Range bypassed overseas supply bottlenecks, allowing Peretti to arrive at Grassroots Outdoor Alliance with high-performing, retail-ready prototypes in hand. events.before: Resources Case Studies Case Study: From Workshop to Moonshot – Xometry's Role in Intuitive Machines' Lunar Return Case Study: From Workshop to Moonshot – Xometry's Role in Intuitive Machines' Lunar Return Written by Nathan Miller 7 min read Published May 7, 2024 Learn how Xometry provided mission-critical CNC machined parts for Intuitive Machines’ lunar lander, Odysseus, helping its engineering team stay on schedule and achieve the first successful American Moon landing in over 50 years. Industries Manufacturing Services Utilized Project Brief Solution Industries Aerospace Manufacturing Services Utilized CNC machining Project Brief NASA tasked Intuitive Machines with building a lunar lander, dubbed Odysseus, that would make the first successful American landing on the Moon since Apollo 17. To meet their fast-approaching deadline, they needed to source hundreds of specialized machined parts quickly. Solution By working with Xometry, Intuitive Machines was able to source hundreds of primer-coated CNC machined parts that held the craft together as it made its descent to the lunar surface. Odysseus touched down safely, began transmitting valuable data to NASA, and helped establish a hopeful precedent for the future of commercial space exploration. Odysseus Sticks the (Lunar) Landing On the evening of February 22, 2024, the Intuitive Machines team waited to see if Odysseus, the lunar lander they spent years building together, had survived its harrowing journey to the Moon’s surface. “On landing day, we were all huddled up out there in the shop staring at the timer – we knew it was going be landing in a couple of minutes,” said Brandon Crain, a procurement manager for Intuitive Machines. Intuitive Machines is a diversified space exploration company focused on pioneering the commercial landscape of outer space and is part of NASA’s Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) initiative . The science and technology payloads sent to the Moon’s surface as part of CLPS are helping lay the foundation for future human missions and a sustainable human presence on the lunar surface. After Odysseus landed, the group continued to wait anxiously. “It's just crickets. Nothing. We're all just waiting,” Crain said. “It was like 10 minutes where we're all wondering, ‘Did it work?’” Credit: Intuitive Machines/ Nick Rios Tim Crain (no relation), chief technology officer at Intuitive Machines, finally shared the news the team was waiting to hear “Alright, guys, we can confirm without a doubt that our hardware is on the surface of the Moon.” The Intuitive Machines team was able to successfully land the Company’s Nova-C class lunar lander on the Moon, marking the United States’ first lunar landing since Apollo 17 more than 50 years ago. “The minute that they could confirm that they had a signal, the place went nuts – it was amazing! Because until that minute, we didn't know [if it survived the landing],” Crain recalled, smiling. “That was a very, very fun night.” For most, Odysseus’ journey began with a rocket launch and ended with a successful landing. For Crain and his team, that night was an exhilarating conclusion to years of hard work and dedication. To the Moon or Bust Credit: Intuitive Machines/ Nick Rios Brandon Crain serves as a liaison between the engineering and purchasing teams at Intuitive Machines. “Once the engineers have parts they need made, they hand them off to me. Hoping to do more hands-on work and achieve a better work-life balance, he started dreaming of owning his own machine shop. Encouraged by a coworker and backed by support from his former employer, Shebesta invested in a 3-axis mill and founded his company in 2023. "I was just thinking about it<dynamic-value>, is this possible? Is this something that I could do?" Shebesta recalled. "From there I was just like, 'Okay, I'm going to take the chance and I'm going to do this.'" After discovering Xometry while sourcing equipment, he joined the Xometry Partner Network in 2024, unlocking the consistent demand he needed to turn his leap of faith into a thriving enterprise. Instant Enterprise Access Close to Home Starting a precision machine shop from scratch often means struggling with cold calls and client acquisition. Partnering with Xometry eliminated that initial barrier entirely. By taking on work through the Xometry Job Board, Shebesta gained immediate access to enterprise-tier accounts. “The work I get from Xometry that I couldn't get on my own would definitely be some of the bigger companies that [order] through Xometry. It's really hard to get your foot in the door with some of these bigger companies,” Shebesta said. Being able to access enterprise-level work for aerospace companies through the Xometry platform is “amazing.” Another key benefit for Shebesta is that Kingdom Precision Machining is located next to his house. Instead of enduring a rigid corporate commute, Shebesta enjoys a combination of hands-on shop work, programming, and quality time with his family. I can see them and wave them goodbye, and then see them when they come back home … Having that freedom as a business owner now is really awesome.” Kingdom Precision Machining owner Sam Shebesta at his shop in Burleson, Texas. Xometry has been very helpful in getting different certifications and things that I need, and equipping me to be in this industry and thrive. That forward-looking investment has paid off: Kingdom Precision Machining has completed 82 jobs and generated over $436,000 in revenue through Xometry. And there's room to grow,” she said. “I’m very excited to see what they've accomplished already, the possibilities, and the role that Xometry has played along the way.” Gollapalli emphasized that Xometry’s focus centers around "the three Cs: capabilities, capacity, and certification." When a supplier prioritizes these three things, scale naturally follows. “We have multitudes of stories where folks have started with one machine in a garage and now are running 30- or 40-machine shops with an incredible growth trajectory,” she said. Shebesta credits Xometry’s hands-on support team with keeping his pipeline running smoothly. events.before: Resources Case Studies Case Study: Xometry’s Precise Laser Tube Cutting Helps Sea Box Build, Scale Up a Big Project for a Defense Customer Case Study: Xometry’s Precise Laser Tube Cutting Helps Sea Box Build, Scale Up a Big Project for a Defense Customer Written by Tricia Contreras 7 min read Published September 27, 2024 Learn how this New Jersey-based small business utilized Xometry’s sheet cutting and laser tube cutting services to build a custom structure from the ground up and quickly scale up production. Industries Manufacturing Services Utilized Project Brief Solution Industries ISO containers and modular buildings for commercial and military customers Manufacturing Services Utilized Sheet cutting and laser tube cutting Project Brief Sea Box relies on its in-house engineers and manufacturers for many of its builds, but a large project on a tight timeline required more parts than they could make in-house. Solution The company turned to Xometry to provide the steel sheet metal and tube components for the ground-up build. Since 1984, Sea Box has designed, customized, and manufactured ISO containers and modular buildings for commercial and military applications. From ready-made containers for storage and shipping to custom-built structures for uses ranging from residential to medical, the New Jersey-based small business has expanded its offerings and workforce over the years. Today, it employs about 350 people, including a team of engineers who design unique solutions to fit customers’ needs. Sea Box designs and manufactures modular buildings that are customizable, connectable, and stackable. (Image Credit: Sea Box) Many of Sea Box’s projects are designed and manufactured in-house, but sometimes a large project requires the company to outsource some of the manufacturing. That was the case for a recent project for a defense customer that needed a custom-built prototype on a short timeline. “The schedule and the sheer number of parts required us to reach outside our normal networks and look for other options,” said Jeff Lucas, a senior project manager at Sea Box. Some of Lucas’ colleagues at Sea Box had used Xometry before to get quotes and place orders for custom parts, and they recommended it as a solution for his project. Lucas needed to order roughly 400 machined parts, including sheet metal and laser-cut tubes, so “instead of going to a shop that specializes in sheet metal and another shop that specializes in just tube cutting, we sent everything we needed over,” Lucas said of Xometry. “It was a one-stop shop.” Instead of going to a shop that specializes in sheet metal and another shop that specializes in just tube cutting, we sent everything we needed over [to Xometry]. It was a one-stop shop. Jeff Lucas Senior Project Manager, Sea Box Building From the Ground Up “For most projects, we start with an existing container, and then we modify that,” Lucas said. “For this project, we built it from the ground up, which required specialty tubes and a whole lot more work, because every single piece of the entire build had to be designed, made and purchased, versus just starting with a container, cutting out the corrugated walls and putting in some framing. Additionally, the tolerances that were required on this project were very, very tight—not quite aerospace, but pretty tight—and so the machining capability and the machine work had to be pretty tight.” With such a detailed design, Lucas knew the project would be complicated to schedule since all the parts would need to arrive in a specific order. Sea Box ordered about 400 machined parts, including sheet metal and laser-cut tubes, from Xometry for a ground-up build for a defense customer. (Image Credit: Sea Box) “Trying to schedule all of them and determine lead times is a major driver of our schedule because we can't build anything if we don't have parts here,” he said. Uploading parts to Xometry and being able to track everything on the Teamspace Dashboard simplified the project by giving Lucas and his team an organized source of information. “Being able to look at a full quote for all the parts, and then being able to pick the lead time that worked with our our schedule made it very easy,” he said. “Anytime a part would ship, we would get a notification and the tracking number. We could go on to the project dashboard and see the status of everything that we've ordered, which is very valuable, being able to track that and have access to certification documents and packing slips and whatever other inspection documents we required. In our particular case, we had some parts that were ITAR, so being able to handle the ITAR stuff as well was a major plus. Everything's kind of at your fingertips. Some of the old-school machine shops don't have that sort of tech.” “Being able to look at a full quote for all the parts, and then being able to pick the lead time that worked with our our schedule made it very easy. Anytime a part would ship, we would get a notification and the tracking number. We could go on to the project dashboard and see the status of everything that we've ordered, which is very valuable. Jeff Lucas Senior Project Manager, Sea Box Tight Tolerances Call for Laser Precision Laser-cut tubes were an integral part of the project because “the tubes make up the full structure of this particular container,” Lucas said. “Shipping containers are held to an ISO standard for size and tolerance, so right off the bat, we have to be able to hold those tolerances. But further, for our customers’ equipment to fit, to meet the ISO standards for tolerances on the ultimate size of the container, and for form, fit, and function, ultimately, these tubes have to be the size, and they have to be held within the tolerances that we require. If they're not, there's one or two things that happen. One is we either have to fix the part or replace the part, which is going to drive the schedule down and drive the cost up because we’ve got to re-make it or re-buy it. Or two, it goes in and ultimately, you end up with something else that ends up being out of tolerance, and that impacts our customers’ integration.” Laser-cut tubes ordered from Xometry were an integral part of this Sea Box project. (Image Credit: Sea Box) For some parts of the project that didn’t have such tight tolerances, Lucas’ team ordered tube steel cut to length directly from the steel mill, knowing they could grind off any excess in-house. But for the parts that needed to be perfectly to spec, the team turned to the laser tube cutting capabilities from Xometry. With Xometry parts, “we can have confidence that they're going to be within the tolerances, they're going to be the material they need to be, and they're going to fit the first time without having to rework any part of the job,” he said. Xometry Has the Laser Tube Cutting Solutions You Need for Your Next Project Xometry offers an extensive range of laser tube cutting services . Laser types utilized include fiber laser or CO2 lasers, depending upon the material and application, allowing for very tight tolerances and the ability to cut through wall thicknesses up to 1/2“ on round, square, or rectangular tubes. We now offer instant quotes for tube cutting and tube bending through the Xometry Instant Quoting Engine®, so it’s simpler than ever to get a quote for your next project. Scaling Up for the Future In addition to the ease of ordering parts and his confidence in knowing they would arrive on time, Lucas credits Xometry with making it easy to reorder parts. Repeating or scaling up a project is simple since “all the parts and all the quotes from the prototype were still in the Xometry database,” he said. “So when a customer says, ‘Hey, we're looking for five more, how fast can you do it?’ I can say [to Xometry], ‘Take everything we already did, multiply it by five and give us the pricing, lead time, and all that stuff,” Lucas said. His team did exactly that after the customer approved the prototype and wanted to scale up the project into production. “For all the different parts, we were able to select the lead times that we were looking for. So for parts that we didn't need until a little bit later in the build, we brought them in later, which obviously had an impact on the cost, and we were able to use the money saved on some of that to expedite the parts we needed earlier. So we were able to get started on our build much earlier than anticipated…We issued something like 10 or 11 different purchase orders, and every single one was on time, so there were no late shipments and we haven't had to rework anything, so we were able to go right into production, which was excellent.” Lucas credits Xometry with keeping the project on track and helping Sea Box be able to scale it up for the future. “We wouldn't have been able to pull this job off in the time frame or even on budget [without Xometry,]” he said. Once this low-rate production run of five units is complete, Sea Box plans to scale up production further in 2025. Part of that effort may include augmenting its order with Xometry to include more parts that are pre-assembled, rather than ordered as separate components and welded together onsite. This change could equate to even more time savings that Sea Box could pass along to their customer. “We wouldn't have been able to pull this job off in the time frame or even on budget [without Xometry]. Jeff Lucas Senior Project Manager, Sea Box Tricia Contreras Tricia is a Senior Content Strategist at Xometry. events.before: Resources Case Studies How SentriLock Overcame Supply Chain Disruption with Prototype-to-Production Support How SentriLock Overcame Supply Chain Disruption with Prototype-to-Production Support Written by Tricia Contreras 3 min read Published August 27, 2025 Xometry’s partnership enabled SentriLock to overcome urgent supply constraints, establish a robust onshore manufacturing process, and achieve measurable gains in cost efficiency and production output. When SentriLock , a leader in real estate lockbox solutions, experienced a critical supply chain disruption, the company turned a business challenge into an opportunity for innovation and operational improvement through a partnership with Xometry. The Challenge: When Supply Chains Break Down SentriLock is a real estate management platform known for its innovative electronic lockboxes that give agents flexible access to properties via codes or the SentriKey® app. As a leader in the industry, SentriLock continually invests in product improvements to maintain its competitive edge and deliver exceptional value to its users. However, the company’s initiative to onshore its manufacturing operations hit a major snag when onshoring a redesign of the lockbox key bin failed validation. The Solution: Prototype-to-Production Partnership With limited time to rework the design and find new suppliers, SentriLock engaged Xometry for support in redesign, prototyping, and scaling domestic production. Will Kefauver, SentriLock’s senior lead product development engineer at the time, explained: “I couldn't have done this without the robustness of Xometry’s partner network. I had a certain budget that had to be met. I had target pricing. And what I really loved about Xometry was I could share those parameters with them and ask, ‘How close can you get?’” Xometry leveraged its extensive supplier network and manufacturing technology to: Use additive manufacturing for initial prototyping and design validation Transition to urethane casting for an efficient ramp-up to full-scale tooling Minimize lead times and support rapid design iteration It is unusual to have the good fortune of lower cost, higher availability, simplified assembly, better reliability and increased production throughput in one part change. You certainly shoot for that, but it is rare to have everything come together where you hit every goal. Xometry was a great partner in working closely with SentriLock’s engineering team to deliver these great results. Scott Fisher CEO, SentriLock Seamless Logistics Support To prevent assembly line downtime, Xometry coordinated a creative logistics solution. Based on the budget requirements, Xometry presented a solution to have the tooling made in China. The process involved manufacturing two months’ worth of injection-molded plastic parts in China, which were air-freighted to the U.S., ensuring continued assembly operations. The injection molding tool itself was then ocean-freighted for setup in the U.S., supporting the transition to domestic production. With all these moving parts, streamlined communication played a crucial role. SentriLock worked through a single point of contact at Xometry, eliminating the miscommunication that can come from using multiple vendors. “I would have had to talk to at least six other vendors if it wasn't for Xometry. The fact that I had just one point of contact made it much more efficient for me,” Kefauver said. Achieving Results: Cost Savings and Increased Production By redesigning the key bin with fewer components and onshoring production, SentriLock achieved significant improvements: 25% reduction in part count, resulting in annual material savings of $780,000 Fewer assembly steps, doubling lockbox production from 700 to 1,300 units daily Scott Fisher, CEO of SentriLock, said: “It is unusual to have the good fortune of lower cost, higher availability, simplified assembly, better reliability and increased production throughput in one part change. You certainly shoot for that, but it is rare to have everything come together where you hit every goal. Xometry was a great partner in working closely with SentriLock’s engineering team to deliver these great results." Tricia Contreras Tricia is a Senior Content Strategist at Xometry. events.before: Resources Supplier Shop Tips How Partners With ITAR Registration Earn More How Partners With ITAR Registration Earn More Written by Tricia Contreras 5 min read Published October 19, 2026 ITAR registration gives Xometry Partners access to high-precision, technical manufacturing work. Here's how to register, what it costs, and how to decide if it's worth it for your shop.
